title: 2026/08/27 - JU
machineSummary: Submitters on the Community Magistrate Legislation Amendment Bill—including Max, Elizabeth (Defence Lawyers Association), Karen Hutchinson, Jo Turner (Community Law Centres), and the Law Association—opposed Clause 22. They said allowing non-legally trained community magistrates to determine guilt in imprisonable Category 2 trials undermines judicial quality and system integrity.

chunks.text: I want to talk primarily about cases that will come before a community magistrate. Not exclusively, but dealing with the profile of young person, female or Māori. I argue that justice that does not recognize an offender as a moral agent is not a good justice system.

The discussion around improvement to the justice system in recent times has been about making social variables part of the assessment in terms of crime and criminality. What has become more prevalent has been the increased dependence on the recognition of particular social, cultural, and political context. I argue that where these elements enter into decisions with regard conviction and sentencings, these disrupt the principles found in our Western system of justice in terms of partiality and objectivity.

My observation is based on the writing of Von Hertz, his censor-based justification for punishment. For both repentant or defied offenders, we would not wish to exempt from blame for either. Both remain moral agents, limiting inquiry to questions about his or her choice to make rational choices.

So I would oppose a view that deemed a group as being unable to make rational choices. In the case involving a truck driver in Taranaki killed by a 13-year-old female using his own hammer, there have been attempts to revisit the crime by lawmakers looking at variables such as age, developmental stage, and cognitive function.

Other cases I will mention is the conviction of sexual offenses by Jayden Meyer, amongst others. If people are called to desist, there must be a good reason for supporting it is wrong. I'm concerned we are breeding a sense of self-entitlement among certain offenders. This is, "I can put myself above others,"

and I argue this is setting up a dangerous precedent in making concessions to popular opinion of writers such as Leffa. Treating an actor as someone capable of choice rather than a circus tiger is a matter of acknowledging his dignity as a human being.

And while we can have some confidence in the moral judgment that offenders should be treated as agents capable of choice, this will not guarantee that this would lead to a more smooth-running society, nor even a society with more social cohesion.

But I reject the notion that it should come at a cost of the case of justice that I am presenting. Thank you, Max. Rima. Thank you. Max, you touched upon the concept of someone having their mental capability. Do you mean the notion that men in particular, women to the age of about 21, but men in particular, their brains are still developing to the age of 25?

Is that what you meant when you touched on development? Yes. So this has been a thought made popular by such writers as Nigel Leffty, and it has gone and infected a lot of society. It's also affected lawmakers in terms of how they look at young offenders.
Yeah. Thank you. Thank you, Max. Thanks for your submission today. We're now going to move to online to the Defense Lawyers Association.

Hi, Elizabeth. Tena koutou katoa. Thank you very much for joining us. We've got you down for 10 minutes. We've read your written submission- Yeah... and just leave some time at the end for questions, please. Yes, of course. I won't take 10 minutes at all. Thank you so much for the opportunity to speak in relation to the Community Magistrate Legislation Amendment Bill.

As you know from our written submission, Te Matakāhi, the Defense Lawyers Association, is a organization that represents criminal defense lawyers and their clients in terms of changes in the criminal justice landscape that may impact on access to justice, fairness, accountability, and a humane and safe approach to criminal matters.

The bill is largely supported by Te Matakāhi in terms of particularly the overall gain of reducing delay and making better use of judicial resources. We don't oppose steps that could achieve that safely. There is one clause in particular that we do oppose, and that's Clause 22, and the written submission focuses on the opposition to that portion of the proposed bill.

I also, of course, have read the submissions that have been put forward by the New Zealand Law Society and the Law Association and other legal bodies, and also speak in support of concerns around the amendments to sections 14 to 17 of the Bail Act, and where guilty pleas to Category 3 offenses Would be contemplated in the reservations that are listed there by the New Zealand Law Society in particular.

If I can though address in the speaking slot now the concerns that we hold around Clause 22, and the concerns come from a number of different angles and perspectives. We are concerned that the impression that is left about New Zealand's Criminal Justice System will be impeded if we have non-legally trained fact finders sitting essentially as judges as community magistrates.

The concept that just because the maximum penalty for something is three months or under means that it's simple and straightforward, is a misnomer. Some of the most complicated issues that affect criminal justice are charges that are, on the face of it, not that serious, but do engage real issues, and our very strong concern is that community magistrates have a very strong place in our criminal justice system, yes, but their place should not be in determining guilt of people where the maximum penalty is still one that

carries imprisonment. And whilst, of course, people can have courses and training, and we recommend and of course support all of that, the reality is that there would be an inconsistent approach taken to the judicial background of different judicial officers in New Zealand.

Family court associates must have seven years as a practicing lawyer. Associate judges of a high court, obviously legal experience and substantive legal experience required. Associate coroners, practice certificates with at least five years. And so this reducing the threshold for community magistrates who have no legal training necessarily is a deep concern with the perception of justice and the delivery of justice.

Our concern is that this impedes on Section 25A of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act in terms of a fair hearing before an independent and impartial court. But also New Zealanders are entitled to expect that judicial officers are legally trained, and by allowing Clause 22 to pass, you are essentially saying that that is not so.

And you just have to step back, I think, as well, and think how members of the public will look at that. If someone has been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment by a community magistrate, the first thing that they will be saying is, "Well, this is rubbish. The person wasn't even a lawyer. They didn't even have a law degree, and now they're going to send me to jail." So I think there's a real concern about, yes, we need efficiency in the criminal justice space, and yes, there's lots in the bill that reduces the burden on judges,

and allowing CMs to have greater scope to take care of administrative matters. Absolutely no problem with that. But this Clause 22 is problematic. And of course, the downstream or the perception of cost savings is also an illusion because all you're doing is shoving the problem down through into appeals, judges having to get involved, and in the process of doing that, you are undermining the reputation of New Zealand's criminal justice system.

So while we're very supportive of large portions of the bill, Clause 22 in particular we see as a very dangerous and unwise inclusion in the bill, and we share our other legal professional organizations that also express the same concern. And as I say, also raise a concern around guilty plea, particularly where it's tied to bail with the community magistrate and the way that the Sections 14 to 17 of the Bail Act and the Category 3 guilty plea in Clause 24 is referenced. The Law Society raises the point that there is a concern that you will be incentivizing people to

plead guilty, and the problems with that are well known and the Chief Justice is incredibly concerned about that happening in New Zealand, and no good comes from it. No good comes from it in terms of our reputation, for the parties involved, or for the cost of undoing and unwinding those sorts of errors. So those are the comments that I'd have to make.

I'm obviously very happy to answer any questions that the committee has. Thank you, Elizabeth. We've got a question from Dan Rosewarne. Yes, thank you so much. Yeah, thanks, Elizabeth. You mentioned so a maximum penalty is not a measure of trial complexity- Correct... and you highlight that it's particularly obvious in driving matters.

Mm-hmm. And I was just wondering if you could, for my own understanding, give me a particular driving charge where that might be applicable? Well, that's the difficult aspect to it, Mr. Rosewarne, because I think that what looks like it might be straightforward from the outside can be very fact specific and can become very complex very quickly. There are lawyers in New Zealand, as you will know, that specialize in traffic matters because of the complexity that's involved in traffic legislation and in some of the factual issues that arise and the

circumstances that arise. So as much as I'd like to give you a short form, "Look, you should look at this section and this section, and these are the types of offenses I'm talking about," that actually isn't, I think, the right way to look at it, as much as I want to be helpful. Because we often find that you go down to court for something that you think is reasonably open and shut, and the next minute you are knee-deep in access to justice, human rights issues- And before you know it, you're in the Court of Appeal.

So, I just think that-- and the danger here that's engaged is that we're talking about imprisonable offenses, and that's the problem. We didn't have as much opposition when community magistrates were doing judge alone, well, judicial officer alone trials, where it was finable only, because there'd be time for review and someone's liberty wasn't at stake.

But where liberty is at stake, it really does, as we say, where the rubber hits the road, and that's where we've got to be super careful. And as I say, as a practitioner for almost 30 years now, I've certainly gone down to court for what I thought would be something that on paper looks relatively straightforward, and neck minute, you're not straightforward at all.

So, yeah. Sorry I can't be more helpful- No, that's, no, you're-... or far outs, but that's kind of the point that I'm making about that. Thank you. Okay, and we've got a question from Camilla Belich. Thanks for your submission. Thank you. I just had a question around, I think the point about liberty is important. The issue that I wanted to get your guidance on is, at the moment I understand we've got around 23 community magistrates and only about eight of them are legally qualified, and I'm not sure if they would be to the extent I think you may have suggested,

seven years for comparable PQE. But the... And I don't know whether they would fall under that or not. But, so would a proposal to kind of further the objective of this legislation, but taking into account your concerns, would you see that if these new powers were only available to those that were legally qualified and the other community magistrates did the other work, would that be a workable solution, or do you- I'm not sure. I'm not sure, Ms. Belich.

I think the problem would be how that judicial resource would then get managed, and then whether you'd end up with a two-tiered approach where you have a community magistrate in, Whangarei that has legal training, but a community magistrate... The community magistrate that covers Wellington Lower Hutt and Porirua comes from a real estate background and has no legal training.

So, then it would become a little bit postcode justice depending on where you were and where your community magistrate sat from. Can I just have a supplementary question on that? So, we have been advised that a way that currently the magistrates lists work is that, because there is a, I can't remember the exact name, is it chief magistrate or the head magistrate- Mm... is able to tailor the lists depending on people's expertise.

Do you have any reflections on whether that's, with these new changes, whether that's likely to be effective in mitigating any of those concerns? I don't, because you're still working from the same pool of numbers and the same small proportion that have legal training. And I think your question might point about, well, what level of legal training, and is there a guidelines and guidance in terms of maybe it should be a certain amount of PQE, and an experience in litigation or an experience in criminal or jurisdiction that might be important there.

So, if we had a situation where community magistrates had legal training and had met a standard of PQE, and there was the complaint process that extended as well to community magistrates, as I know the Law Society has suggested in their submission, then that might alleviate some of the concerns.

Absolutely. Because the concern is that you've got non-legally trained people exercising the power to imprison. But unless we had that change, I'm afraid my position would still be that we should just not extend Clause 22, and that maybe it's something that we come back to if the community magistrates become people who are legally trained.

Thank you. Thank you, Elizabeth. Really appreciate your time this afternoon and your written submission as well. Thank you so much. Thanks. Okay, now we've got Community Law Centres Aotearoa, and they're joining us online as well.

Hey, Karen. Thank you for joining us this afternoon. We have read your written submission, and we've got you down for 10 minutes. Over to you. Great. Thank you. I'm just checking if Jo... I'm meant to be here with Jo Turner, but I'm not sure if she's online yet. No, it doesn't. Well, I will get going, and we'll see- Thank you... what happens. Tena koutou, members of the committee. Tena koe, Mr. Chair.

Thank you for this opportunity to submit today. You'll know that I'm Karen Hutchinson, as written down. I'm a law reform coordinator at CLCA, which means that I take all the feedback from our community lawyers on the ground and bring that to you, as select committee on changes to the law. I'm here with Jo Turner. I can see that she is there.

I am here. I'm just having- Let me pull up Jo... some technical problems, sorry. That's okay. I'm here with Jo, and she is a solicitor at Otago Community Law and has extensive experience in criminal law as a criminal lawyer. I'll summarize our submissions and leave time for questions. We are the national body that coordinates and advocates for 24 community law centers across the country. Community law centers routinely provide initial legal advice on criminal law matters, and some of our lawyers do criminal defense work.

It's number three on the areas of work that community lawyers do in our movement after employment and care of children. We agree that measures are needed to improve timeliness across the district court, but our submissions outline that we're concerned that access to justice is compromised in the pursuit of timeliness in this bill.

We made some high-level submissions on the bill on the following points. Our experience is that community magistrate days in the district court are really heavy in terms of workload and long waits, and understand that there's a few more magistrates potentially on the way. But we've recommended that if there is to be greater work, then there needs to be some more time for them to sit.

The bill, in our view, essentially moves that chunk of work, the backlog that's sitting there, or the clog that's sitting there from judges to community magistrates without making more room for them. Increasing capacity and speed at this part of the criminal justice system is likely to create pressure on other parts of the system, prosecutors, corrections, legal aid and duty lawyers.

And I note too, I've just seen from the chief judge's submission that she's recommended that there be a first principles review for increasing capacity in the district court. That sounds like a really comprehensive way forward rather than addressing things in this way with this bill.

Similar to the previous submitter, Ms. Hall, you'll know not all community magistrates are required to hold a legal qualification and have practice experience. This is of real concern to us in relation to Clause 22, for increased jurisdiction to preside over Category 2 offenses with a term of imprisonment not exceeding three months.

For this reason in particular, the presumption or the ... Sorry, the perception of what that will look like for our criminal justice system and also any difficulties that are encountered in terms of the expertise and the skill and the judgment that's required, and any missteps in those ways is likely to affect those groups that are over-represented, including Maori and Pacifica people. We have concerned about the expanded bail jurisdiction, given that ultimately that decision rests with a judge at the moment, and we don't believe that those decisions

should be extended. We support the appointment of a principal community magistrate, and that they must be a district court judge. We wonder whether that should be an additional district court judge rather than trying to put that job on a district court judge, given how busy they are. Given the access to justice issues raised in our submissions and by others, including The Law Society, TLANZ, Te Hunga Roa Maori, and the defense lawyers group before us, there should really be a mechanism to monitor how these changes play out,

and that there be a statutory review if the bill is to go ahead in its current form. And just a point about the potential for community magistrates to need to be required to hold legal qualifications should these extended powers go ahead. Family court associates and other judicial officers need to have those qualifications, and we believe that in this situation, they should have those qualifications as well.

And that's really all I have from our submissions. And if there's any questions, we'd love to hear them from you. Duncan. Kia ora. Good to see you, as always. Thanks for all your work you do on this law reform stuff. I guess I want to ask a question that's kind of been nagging away, and it's not a very polite one.

But is there a quality problem with community magistrates? I understand the whole idea of giving citizen magistrates some modest powers to direct traffic in the district courts. But when they come to make decisions in hard law, are they any good at it? And you're much closer to the coalface than I am, because I have concerns in extending powers if what we see already is poor quality justice kind of done on the cheap.

So it's a bit of a tough question, but I'd be really interested in an honest answer. I'll leave that to Jo. Do you have anything, Jo? Yeah. The community magistrates that come to Dunedin are all really lovely people and do a great job, but their ways of approaching the various issues are quite different. They're not always the way you would expect a judge to approach it.

So there is a difference in kind of expertise or comfortness in that area. Some community magistrates read... Well, it comes across like they're reading a script. Which can be problematic because it's all pre-written and pre-decided. So I think there are issues around quality, and that really lies at our concerns around the increased jurisdiction.

When you're getting these people to make decisions of a more serious nature, then the risks are much higher that they get it wrong Thanks for that. That's really useful. Okay. Thank you very much, Karen, and thank you, Joe, as well. Really appreciate both of you joining us this afternoon. Thank you. Kia ora. Ka kite.
Okay. We've got our last submission from the Law Association of New Zealand, who are joining us online as well.

Good afternoon, all. Hello. We can't see you at present. Switch it up screen. Oh, there you go. You can see me now. Great. We've got you down for 10 minutes. We've read your written submission. Over to you. Thank you. Thank you, Chair, and the members of the committee. Of course, I appear on behalf of the Law Association.

Both the Criminal Law Committee and the Public and Administrative Law Committee made submissions on the bill. Look, we support the objective of the bill. We do recognize that there's serious pressure and delays facing the District Court. We seriously support the Chief Community Magistrate. Judge Moses is very experienced, and we are very happy that he's been appointed to the role, and we will support him in any capacity we can. But there's one aspect of this bill that we strongly oppose, and that's quite consistent with all the other associations

who have made submissions. So I really want to concentrate on that today as opposed to all the other aspects of the bill, which we have put in our written submissions. And Duncan, I would like you to ask me the same question you asked other speakers in terms of what we see on the ground, because I do have a good answer for you on that, because we do deal with CMs quite extensively- Well, consider it asked... across the country.

Consider it asked. Yes, I will answer it at the end. So look, our main issue is around giving community magistrates jurisdiction to preside over trials on Category 2 offendings and determining guilt, when the offense carries up to three months imprisonment.

I was heavily involved during the consultation process, and during that time, we actually said that the magistrate should not do judge-alone trials for anything other than fine-only matters. But once the Parliament moves beyond the fine-only offending and allows a person who's not required to be legally qualified to determine contested criminal guilt for something which is imprisonable, whether it's three months or not, we say an important constitutional and institutional boundary has been crossed.
What you may think is that because the offense carries up to three months imprisonment, it doesn't mean it's necessarily simple offending. It's actually exactly the opposite. So-

Oh, lost her I think I was- Samira... I think I was cut off. Can you hear me now? We can. We lost you for the last 30 seconds. Okay. All right. If you just give me one second, I will probably use this other connection. Yeah. But you can just- Okay. Sorry... turn your camera off. Maybe it would save some- Maybe... internet.

Okay. I should be all good from now. Sorry. So I'm just going to go back a little bit, just 30 seconds. I was giving you an example in terms of offenses under Category 2 for up to three months, and I was going to focus on, for example, drunk drive offending, careless driving causing injury, or careless driving causing death.

So these type of offending, let's focus on one, which is drunk driving. They can involve highly technical questions concerning a statutory interpretation, procedural compliance, evidential presumptions, admissibility, improperly obtained evidence, identification, expert or technical evidence of the Land Transport Act, the Evidence Act, and appellate authority.

So the judicial officer must be able to identify these issues. And I can tell you this, even if you ask other very experienced trial lawyers, it's a lot easier to run a trial for an aggravated robbery or a burglary as opposed to a three-month imprisonment drunk drive charge.

The technicality involved in these offendings are so much that even with a District Court judge, we sometimes have to get into statutory interpretation and explain to the judge why this clause applies or why that clause applies. And if you remember a few years ago over the Block J defense in a first-time drunk drive, we had to go to the Supreme Court because that involved a question of law. So you're not necessarily dealing with simple offending just because it carries maximum three months imprisonment. That is the first point that we would

raise. So the maximum penalty measures the seriousness Parliament attaches to an offense. It doesn't measure the complexity of the trial. So I really invite you all to get more information on how technical these trials can get. Then we have the issue of institutional anomaly here. So I would ask the question: Why do we have associate employment judges, associate family court judges, associate high court judges, and they come from a legally qualified background with years and years in practice.

Whereas in criminal law, we are appointing people doing trials when they are not legally qualified or where they haven't practiced at all in the past. So that's another point that we have raised. The point that I just wanted to mention, which was not in our submissions, the Regulatory impact statement from the consultation which happened in 2023, says that imprisonment and home detention are core judicial functions that only judges should undertake, and yet you have decided to determining guilt and convicting someone by way of a trial is not a core

judicial function, and it can be done by someone who's not legally qualified. So that is a very important distinction here that you need to be able to make. The same RIS records that the judiciary and other legal professionals raised substantive concerns over the expansion of the jurisdiction of the community magistrates at the time.

I do not understand between 2023 and 2025, where the bill has been introduced, what has changed. Because nothing really has changed in respect of the consultation that was conducted two years ago, three years ago, with the profession and with the judiciary. And the profession and the judiciary all raised concerns over the same issues, which is now implemented in the current bill, including the magistrates presiding over judge-alone trials.

So we really don't know what has been done to address those concerns. You're doing this to avoid a backlog, okay? But it's going to be very counterproductive because you're going to end up with so many appeals. So you're not going to actually free up judges from doing less cases. Not only they have to deal with their own cases, but now they have to deal with appeals after appeals.

I also- I'm just going to say you've got about 30 more seconds. Yeah. I'm going to cut it short. Cut it short, because we have put most of our objections in our submissions, but long story short is this: as long as you remove the expansion of jurisdiction for them to preside over trials, I think that potentially the rest of the objections that have been raised by us and other associations to an extent could be addressed and could be moderated. But there's nothing we can suggest to make it better in terms of them presiding over a judge-alone

trial. That needs to be completely removed from the bill, and that needs to stay with the judge. Okay, thank you very much for your time this afternoon and for the written submission that you submitted as well. Really appreciate it. Thank you. No problem. Can I just quickly answer Duncan's question very briefly in 20 seconds? Duncan, you ask how they operate on the ground. Jo answered the question quite well.

Sometimes it comes across as they are reading from a transcript. That means they have typed it up for themselves, and they're reading from it in terms of giving a decision, which is kind of concerning. It doesn't affect the fact that they're lovely people, they're really good people to appear before. But one thing that we come across quite regularly in court, as soon as they're out of their comfort zone, as soon as they're out of the comfort zone in the sense that, "Oh, I don't know the answer to this," things just get very complicated in court.

Yeah. And then explaining to them what the law is, what the statutory interpretation of that section is, what is the correlation between the Land Transport Act, for example, and the Evidence Act or the Sentencing Act, it becomes too confusing for them. And of course, it becomes very complicated for the lawyer, which means we have to adjourn the case and either get the matter dealt with by a judge or try to make further submissions so they can go and talk to a district court judge to make a decision. So, yeah, that's the answer to your question.
Thank you for that. Thank you. Thank you very much. My pleasure. Thank you, everyone. See ya. Thanks. Okay, we're going to move into private now. If our advisors come forward, please
